questions.question_text: In which of the following age groups is the prevalence of depression in males equivalent to that in females?
questions.explanation:
The prevalence of depression in pre-pubertal children is approximately 1-2%, with no sex diVerence. By mid-teens, the prevalence is around 4-5%, with the female predominance characteristic of adult depression clearly established.
Ref: Maughan B et al. Depression in childhood and adolescence. Journal of the Canadian Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. 2013 Feb;22(1):35.

questions.question_text: In the management of encopresis, which mode of treatment uses operant techniques such as star charts?
questions.explanation:
Most cases of encopresis have multifactorial causes. Possible elements of treatment include:
●      Lifestyle changes (e.g., adequate buid and dietary `bre)
●      Evacuate stool; laxatives may be used to prevent further retention.
●      Education of the child and family, and assistance to view the child more positively.
●      Behavioural therapy – operant training with rewards and positive reinforcement (e.g., star charts)
●      Family therapy: reduce family tensions and establish a nonpunitive atmosphere (e.g., Sneaky Poo – a narrative therapy and externalising approach that helps unite the family against the problem of soiling, which is personi`ed as the character 'Sneaky Poo')
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 681, 908.

questions.question_text: What genetic aetiology most increases the risk of parents having a second child with Down syndrome?
questions.explanation:
In translocation, a fusion occurs of two chromosomes, usually 21 and 15, resulting in a total of 46 chromosomes, despite the presence of one extra chromosome 21. Unlike trisomy 21, this is usually inherited, and the translocated chromosome may be found in unaVected parents or siblings (who only have 45 chromosomes).
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 101.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not recommended in the management of anxiety disorders in children and adolescents?
questions.explanation:
For the treatment of anxiety disorders in children and adolescents, psychoeducation can help families understand the condition and provide reassurance. CBT has been proven to be effective, incorporating both cognitive (e.g. reframing, positive self-talk, challenging unhelpful thoughts, and weighing up evidence for and against expected events) and behavioural processes (e.g. systematic desensitisation, exposure and response prevention for speci`c phobias, relaxation training, modelling, rewarding wanted behaviour, and role-play). Family therapy may help when dysfunctional patterns of family interaction influence the child's anxiety symptoms. SSRIs can be effective and are generally well-tolerated. Medication is usually most considered in older children with more severe symptoms. Benzodiazepines have NOT shown emcacy; their side eVects (e.g. behavioural disinhibition) are a risk in this population.
Ref: Vallance AK, Fernandez V. Anxiety disorders in children and adolescents: aetiology, diagnosis and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2016 Sep;22(5):335-44.

questions.question_text: The rate of self-harm in teenagers who identify with Goth culture is around
questions.explanation:
About half of 'Alternative' (e.g. Goth) adolescents self-injure, primarily to regulate emotions and communicate distress.
Ref: Young R, Sproeber N, Groschwitz RC, Preiss M, Plener PL. Why alternative teenagers self-harm: exploring the link between non-suicidal self-injury, attempted suicide and adolescent identity. BMC psychiatry. 2014 Dec 1;14(1):137.

questions.question_text: In a child with developmental disturbances, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis. The diagnosis is most likely to be
questions.explanation:
Children with cerebellar vermal agenesis or diVuse cerebellar hypoplasia commonly present with core autistic spectrum disorder symptoms including language de`cits, social interaction impairments, and repetitive and stereotyped behaviours.
Ref: Hampson DR, Blatt GJ. Autism spectrum disorders and neuropathology of the cerebellum. Frontiers in neuroscience. 2015 Nov 6;9:420.

questions.question_text: Tourette syndrome is characterised by all except

options.text: Symptoms present for at least a year
Mean age of onset = seven years
Seen more commonly in girls than boys

correct_answer.text: Seen more commonly in girls than boys

correct_answers.text: Seen more commonly in girls than boys

questions.explanation:
Tourette syndrome is a complex neuropsychiatric disorder with childhood onset characterised by multiple motor and one or more vocal tics, present for at least a year. Males are more commonly aVected (3-4:1, male:female). The age of onset is 2-21 years, with a mean age of 7 years.
Ref: Robertson MM. Tourette syndrome in children and adolescents: aetiology, presentation and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2016 May;22(3):165-75.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 587.

questions.question_text: Which of the following genetic disorders is most closely associated with autism?
questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability(ID). It accounts for 10-12% of ID in men. Mild ID is often seen in aVected women whereas moderate/severe ID is seen in aVected men. There are high rates of ADHD and autism spectrum disorder in Fragile X syndrome.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 814.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 102.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is recommended as a `rst-line, evidence-based treatment for anorexia nervosa?
questions.explanation: Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. NICE guideline Eating Disorders: recognition and treatment 2017.

questions.question_text: The male to female ratio for conduct disorder is
questions.explanation:
The worldwide prevalence of conduct disorder (CD) is estimated to be 2-2.5%, with a prevalence of 3-4% in boys and 1-2% in girls. CD is approximately twice as common in males as in females and this `nding has been observed across geographical regions. Despite major cultural diVerences in what is considered acceptable childhood behaviour, there is little evidence suggesting that the prevalence of CD diVers between countries.
Ref: Fairchild G et al. Conduct disorder. Nature Reviews Disease Primers. 2019 Jun 27;5(1):1-25.

questions.question_text: In ICD-11, enuresis is de`ned as the repeated involuntary or voluntary voiding of urine into clothes or bed for a child of age
questions.explanation:
In ICD-11, enuresis is de`ned as the repeated voiding of urine into clothes or bed, which may occur during the day or at night, in an individual who has reached a developmental age when urinary continence is ordinarily expected (5years). Voiding of urine is typically involuntary but, in some cases, may appear to be voluntary. The diagnosis can be assigned in either case.
Ref: International Statistical Classi`cation of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about childhood elimination disorders is correct?

options.text: Star charts are helpful in encopresis but not in enuresis
Secondary enuresis is an atypical extension of normal infantile incontinence
Nocturnal enuresis occurs more commonly in girls than in boys
Functional encopresis is unrelated to sleep disorders
Enuresis may occur in association with a mental disorder or psychosocial stressor

correct_answer.text: Enuresis may occur in association with a mental disorder or psychosocial stressor

correct_answers.text: Enuresis may occur in association with a mental disorder or psychosocial stressor

questions.explanation:
In ICD-11, enuresis is de`ned as the repeated voiding of urine into clothes or bed, which may occur during the day or at night, in an individual who has reached a developmental age when urinary continence is ordinarily expected (5 years). The urinary incontinence may have been present from birth (i.e., an atypical extension of normal infantile incontinence), or may have arisen following a period of acquired bladder control ('secondary' or 'previously dry' enuresis). The common age of onset for children who have previously acquired urinary continence, yet develop enuresis, is between the ages of 5 to 8 years. Nocturnal enuresis is more common in males, whereas diurnal enuresis is more common in females. Enuresis may be an aspect of another mental, behavioural, or neurodevelopmental disorder. Psychosocial stressors appear to precipitate enuresis in a subgroup of children with the disorder. In young children, the disorder may relate to the birth of a sibling, hospitalisation, the start of school, separation of a family due to divorce, or a move to a new environment.
Ref: International Statistical Classi`cation of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 680.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 485.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with respect to enuresis?

options.text: It is always accompanied by encopresis
Diurnal enuresis is more common in boys than girls
It cannot be diagnosed without anatomical scan of urinary tract
It does not occur as an aspect of a mental disorder

questions.explanation:
In ICD-11, enuresis is de`ned as the repeated voiding of urine into clothes or bed, which may occur during the day or at night, in an individual who has reached a developmental age when urinary continence is ordinarily expected (5 years). Nocturnal enuresis is more common in males, whereas diurnal enuresis is more common in females. Enuresis is more common among children with a parent who has a history of enuresis. Enuresis may be an aspect of another mental, behavioural, or neurodevelopmental disorder. Psychosocial stressors appear to precipitate enuresis in a subgroup of children with the disorder. In young children, the disorder may relate to the birth of a sibling, hospitalisation, the start of school, separation of a family due to divorce, or a move to a new environment.
Ref: International Statistical Classi`cation of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 680.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 485.

questions.question_text: Compared to adult-onset schizophrenia, early-onset schizophrenia is associated with
questions.explanation:
Early-onset schizophrenia is associated with poor premorbid functioning and early developmental delays. Crystallised knowledge and global IQ appear to be more impaired in early-onset schizophrenia cases than in adult-onset cases. A consistent characteristic is impaired sociability, with significant premorbid dimculties in social development affecting the ability to make and keep friends. Early-onset schizophrenia is characterised by a more insidious onset, negative symptoms, greater disorganisation (incoherence of thought and disordered sense of self), hallucinations in different modalities and, for relatively fewer patients, systematised or persecutory delusions. It typically has a chronic, unremitting long-term course, with severely impaired functioning in adult life. The long-term outcome is generally poor, but there is heterogeneity.
Ref: Driver DI, Thomas S, Gogtay N, Rapoport JL. Childhood-onset schizophrenia and early-onset schizophrenia spectrum disorders: an update. Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Clinics. 2020 Jan 1;29(1):71-90.
Harvey PD, Isner EC. Cognition, social cognition, and functional capacity in early-onset schizophrenia. Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Clinics. 2020 Jan 1;29(1):171-82.

questions.question_text: What is the strongest risk factor for criminality at age 17 in a boy who has behavioural problems at the age of 8?
questions.explanation:
Harsh, punitive parenting characterised by severe physical and verbal aggression is associated with the development of aggressive behaviours. Chaotic home conditions are associated with delinquency. Assaultive behaviour in childhood and parental criminality predict a high risk for incarceration later in life.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 192-193.

questions.question_text: A 5-year-old child who has been placed in multiple foster care homes since the age of 2 now shows little regard to seek approval from an adult caregiver before wandering away and a notable willingness to go oV with unfamiliar adults with little hesitation. In ICD-11, these are core features of
questions.explanation:
Disinhibited social engagement disorder (DSED) is newly described in both DSM-5 and ICD-11. It is characterised by grossly abnormal social behaviour, occurring in the context of a history of grossly inadequate child care (e.g., severe neglect, institutional deprivation). These children typically display reduced/absent reticence in approaching/interacting with unfamiliar adults; overly familiar verbal of physical behaviour; diminished/absent checking back with an adult caregiver; and willingness to go oV with unfamiliar adults with little to no hesitation. In contrast to reactive attachment disorder, symptoms of DSED tend to be more persistent following the provision of appropriate care. Children with DSED related to repetitive maltreatment (e.g., chronic physical or sexual abuse) are at risk for developing co-occurring PTSD or complex PTSD. General impulsivity is commonly associated with DSED, and there is a high rate of co-occurrence with ADHD.
Ref: International Statistical Classi`cation of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Separation anxiety disorder (SAD) is characterised by developmentally inappropriate and excessive anxiety concerning separation from home or from those to whom the individual is attached. This condition occurs in about
questions.explanation:
Separation anxiety disorder is characterised by increased and inappropriate anxiety around separation from attachment `gures or home, which is developmentally abnormal and results in impaired functioning. It occurs in about 3.5% of children and 0.8% of adolescents. Symptoms include anxiety about actual or anticipated separation from, or danger to, attachment `gures; sleep disturbances and nightmares; somatisation; and school refusal.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 684.

questions.question_text: According to DSM-5 criteria, the core symptoms of ADHD must have their onset before the age of
questions.explanation:
DSM-5 criteria state that several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms must be present prior to the age of 12 years, and allows for the diagnosis in adults.
Ref: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (DSM-5®). American Psychiatric Pub; 2013 May 22.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 668.

questions.question_text: In ICD-11, a chronic tic disorder can be diagnosed only if tics have been present for at least
questions.explanation:
In ICD-11, chronic (motor or phonic) tic disorders are characterised by the presence of tics over a period of at least one year, although they may not manifest consistently. Motor tics are de`ned as sudden, rapid, non-rhythmic, and recurrent movements. Phonic (vocal) tics are de`ned as sudden, rapid, non-rhythmic, and recurrent vocalisations. To capture patients with motor and/or vocal tics that have been present for less than 12 months in a row, the DSM-5 employs the category of provisional tic disorder (307.21) while ICD-11 uses the term 'transient' (8A05.03: Transient motor tics).
Ref: International Statistical Classi`cation of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)
Cavannaa AE. Tourette syndrome: Current nosology and guidelines. The Neurobiology of the Gilles De La Tourette Syndrome and Chronic Tics: Part A. 2022 Jul 6:103.

questions.question_text: Which of the following positive symptoms is most commonly found in childhood-onset schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Given the rarity of childhood-onset schizophrenia (COS), psychopathological studies are scarce. In one study, 95% of patients with COS had auditory hallucinations, 80% had visual hallucinations. Delusions were noted in 60% of patients. Of these features, presence of delusions and thought disorders predicted a non-aVective psychosis in another study. In adolescent-onset schizophrenia, bizarre behaviour (disorganisation) and negative symptoms may be higher in prevalence than in adult onset, but still the most common symptom appears to be auditory hallucinations.
Ref: Ballageer T, Malla A, Manchanda R, Takhar J, Haricharan R. Is adolescent-onset `rst-episode psychosis diVerent from adult onset?. Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry. 2005 Aug 1;44(8):782-9.
Timn PA, Kitchen CE. Incidence and 12-month outcome of childhood non-aVective psychoses: British national surveillance study. The British Journal of Psychiatry. 2015 Jun;206(6):517-8.
David CN, Greenstein D, Clasen L, Gochman P, Miller R, Tossell JW, Mattai AA, Gogtay N, Rapoport JL. Childhood onset schizophrenia: high rate of visual hallucinations. Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry. 2011 Jul 1;50(7):681-6.

questions.question_text: An adolescent patient diagnosed with ADHD is found to have a co-morbid bipolar disorder. All of the following symptoms could be explained by either diagnosis except
questions.explanation:
ADHD can co-occur with mood disorders, such as bipolar disorder, while inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity can also be features of mood disorders in individuals without ADHD. Symptoms such as restlessness, pacing, and impaired concentration can be features of a depressive episode. Inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity are typical features of manic and hypomanic episodes. At the same time, mood lability and irritability may be associated features of ADHD.
Ref: International Statistical Classi`cation of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: With respect to the delayed development of empathy skills, which of the following is correct?

options.text: Most delayed in hearing children of hearing parents
Most delayed in adopted children of deaf parents
Most delayed in hearing children of hearing parents
Most delayed in deaf children of hearing parents
Most delayed in deaf children of deaf parents

correct_answer.text: Most delayed in deaf children of hearing parents

correct_answers.text: Most delayed in deaf children of hearing parents

questions.explanation:
Deaf preadolescents have more dimculty with empathy development than hearing children, and this ability is related to the onset of deafness (Bachara, 1980). Deaf children born to deaf parents are better in the following areas compared to those born to hearing parents: 1. maturity 2. independence 3. responsibility taking 4. impulse control 5. empathizing ability 6. better match of parental expectations and achievements.
Ref: Bachara, GH. Empathy development in deaf preadolescents. American Annals of the Deaf, 125; 38-41 Feb 1980.
Moores, DF and Meadow-Orlans, KP (ed). Educational and Developmental Aspects of Deafness. Gallaudet University Press 1990. Page 291-93
Peterson CC. Empathy and theory of mind in deaf and hearing children. Journal of deaf studies and deaf education. 2016 Apr 1;21(2):141-7.

questions.question_text: Of the following, the condition most commonly co-morbid with autism spectrum disorders is
questions.explanation:
Frequent co-morbidities in autism spectrum disorders are intellectual disability(80%), anxiety disorders (40-84%), ADHD (30-50%), OCD, and tic disorders.
Ref: Santosh PJ, Singh J. Drug treatment of autism spectrum disorder and its comorbidities in children and adolescents. BJPsych Advances. 2016 May;22(3):151-61.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 674.
Leitner Y. The co-occurrence of autism and attention de`cit hyperactivity disorder in children–what do we know?. Frontiers in human neuroscience. 2014 Apr 29;8:268.

questions.question_text: What is the chance of a 12-year-old boy with conduct disorder developing antisocial personality disorder?
questions.explanation:
Around half of children with conduct disorder will receive a diagnosis of antisocial personality disorder as adults. Substance misuse is also commonly seen in adult life. There is an increased risk of early death, often by violent and sudden means.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 665.

questions.question_text: A 12 yr old boy is found to be skipping school repeatedly and staying out at night to use drugs with his friends. He is most likely to have which of the following psychiatric conditions?
questions.explanation:
Conduct disorder is a repetitive and persistent pattern of antisocial, aggressive, or de`ant behaviours that defy age-appropriate societal norms or rules. Children with conduct disorder are likely to demonstrate behaviours in the following four categories:
o   Aggression to people and animals (e.g. bullies, initiates `ghts, uses a weapon, physical cruelty or people or animals, mugging/robbery, forcing someone into sexual activity)
o   Destruction of property (e.g. `re setting or other methods of destruction)
o   Deceitfulness or theft (e.g. breaking into houses/cars, conning others, shoplifting/forgery)
o   Serious violations of rules (e.g. staying out at night, running away, school truancy)
Ref: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (DSM-5®). American Psychiatric Pub; 2013 May 22.

questions.question_text: You are seeing a 2-year-old boy in the clinic whose vocabulary is limited to only four words (mama, daddy, hi, and more). He rarely communicates but uses these words one at a time in appropriate situations. He supplements his infrequent verbal communications with pointing and other simple gestures to request desired objects or actions. What would be the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Developmental learning disorder with impairment in mathematics
Developmental learning disorder with impairment in reading
Developmental language disorder with impairment of receptive and expressive language
Developmental language disorder with impairment of mainly expressive language
Developmental learning disorder with impairment in written expression

correct_answer.text: Developmental language disorder with impairment of mainly expressive language

correct_answers.text: Developmental language disorder with impairment of mainly expressive language

questions.explanation:
Developmental language disorder with impairment of mainly expressive language is characterised by persistent difficulties in the acquisition, production, and use of language that arise during the developmental period, typically during early childhood, and cause significant limitations in the individual's ability to communicate. The ability to produce and use spoken or signed language (i.e., expressive language) is markedly below the expected level given the individual's age and level of intellectual functioning, but the ability to understand spoken or signed language (i.e., receptive language) is relatively intact.
Ref: International Statistical Classi`cation of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: The risk factors common to children and adolescents who attempt suicide include all except
questions.explanation:
Adolescents who make cognitive errors (e.g. catastrophizing, personalisation) are at increased risk of attempting suicide.
Ref: Spirito A, Esposito-Smythers C, WolV J, Uhl K. Cognitive-behavioral therapy for adolescent depression and suicidality. Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Clinics. 2011 Apr 1;20(2):191-204.

questions.question_text: Of those listed, which is the most common co-morbid psychiatric disorder seen in children with ADHD?
questions.explanation:
50-80% of children with ADHD have a comorbid disorder. Common comorbid conditions include speci`c learning disorders (70%), autism spectrum disorder (59%), tic disorders/Tourette syndrome (55%), oppositional de`ant disorder (30-50%) depression (12-50%), bipolar disorder (5-47%), anxiety disorders (15-35%), conduct disorder (3.5-10%), sleep disorders, and substance misuse.
Ref: Hill P. Attention-de`cit hyperactivity disorder in children and adolescents: Assessment and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jan;21(1):23-30.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 668.
Gnanavel S et al. Attention de`cit hyperactivity disorder and comorbidity: A review of literature. World Journal of Clinical Cases. 2019 Sep 6;7(17):2420.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a core diagnostic feature of ADHD?
questions.explanation:
ADHD is characterised by the three core symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsiveness. Inattention includes being careless with detail, failing to sustain attention, appearing not to listen, failing to `nish tasks, poor self-organisation, losing things, being forgetful, being easily distracted, and avoiding tasks requiring sustained attention. Hyperactivity is most evident in structured situations and includes `dgeting with hands or feet, leaving one's seat in class, running/climbing about, the inability to play quietly, and being 'always on the go'. Impulsiveness includes talking excessively, blurting out answers, the inability to wait one's turn, interrupting others, and intruding on others.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 668.

questions.question_text: Classically, children with enuresis have shown improvement with which one of the following antidepressants?
questions.explanation:
Antidepressants, particularly imipramine, were the `rst medications used for enuresis, and are still used at times to take advantage of their anticholinergic side eVects. However, imipramine does have a considerable side eVect pro`le. Reboxetine, a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor that has a non-cardiotoxic side eVect pro`le, may be a safer alternative to the classically used imipramine in the treatment of childhood enuresis.
Ref: Caldwell PH et al. Tricyclic and related drugs for nocturnal enuresis in children. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016(1).
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 484.

questions.question_text: Of the following, what is the common reason for parents and children to seek treatment for separation anxiety disorder?
questions.explanation:
Worries in separation anxiety disorder often take the form of school refusal, fears and distress on separation, repeated complaints of physical symptoms such as headaches and stomachaches when separation is anticipated, and nightmares related to separation issues. Psychophysiological symptoms include stomachaches, headaches, nausea, vomiting, palpitations, and dizziness when anticipating separation.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 195-198.

questions.question_text: In the very-early-onset variant of schizophrenia, the onset of symptoms is before age
questions.explanation:
Childhood-onset schizophrenia (COS; also called very-early-onset schizophrenia), a very rare and severe chronic psychiatric condition, is de`ned by an onset of positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, and disorganised speech or behaviour) before the age of 13. COS is associated with other neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and attention de`cit and hyperactivity disorder. Copy number variations represent well documented neurodevelopmental disorder risk factors and, recently, de novo single nucleotide variations in genes involved in brain development have also been implicated in the complex genetic architecture of COS.
Ref: Fernandez A et al. Childhood-onset schizophrenia: a systematic overview of its genetic heterogeneity from classical studies to the genomic era. Frontiers in Genetics. 2019 Dec 18;10:1137.
Da Fonseca D, Fourneret P. Very early onset schizophrenia. L'encephale. 2018 Dec 1;44(6S):S8-11.

questions.question_text: Heller syndrome is characterised by marked regression in several areas of functioning after at least how many years of normal development?
questions.explanation:
Childhood disintegrative disorder, also called Heller syndrome and disintegrative psychosis, was `rst described in 1908 as a deterioration over several months of intellectual, social, and language function occurring in 3- and 4-years-old with previously normal function. After the deterioration, the children closely resembled children with autistic disorder. Childhood disintegrative disorder is characterised by marked regression in several areas of functioning after at least 2 years of apparently normal development.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 103.

questions.question_text: A 15-year-old boy has moderate depression and no suicidality. He is a good student and has stable family support. The most suitable `rst-line treatment is
questions.explanation:
For the treatment of moderate-severe depression in young people aged 12-18 years, oVer individual CBT for at least 3 months (if unsuitable, consider IPT for adolescents, family therapy, brief psychosocial intervention, or psychodynamic psychotherapy). Consider combination treatment (buoxetine and psychological therapy) for initial treatment as an alternative to psychological therapy.
Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on the identification and management of depression in children and young people. 2019.

questions.question_text: Which of the following scales could be used in epidemiological studies as a screening tool for caseness among school-going children before further diagnostic procedures?
questions.explanation:
The Strengths and Dimculties Questionnaire is a brief emotional and behaviour screening questionnaire for children and young people that can capture the perspective of children and young people, their parents and teachers. Subscales include: emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity/inattention, peer relationships problem, and prosocial behaviour.
Ref: https://www.corc.uk.net/outcome-experience-measures/strengths-and-dimculties-questionnaire/

questions.question_text: Autism spectrum disorder is typically `rst diagnosed in
questions.explanation:
As noted in ICD-11, characteristic features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) may emerge during infancy although they may only be recognised as indicative of ASD in retrospect. It is usually possible to make the diagnosis of ASD during the preschool period (up to 4 years), especially in children exhibiting developmental delay. ASD is typically evident during the second year of life, and in severe cases, a lack of developmentally appropriate social interactions may be noted even in the `rst year. However, in milder cases, core impairments in ASD may not be identi`ed for several more years.
Ref: International Statistical Classi`cation of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 122.

questions.question_text: Miss. X is a 16-year-old girl who was assessed in the CAMHS outpatient clinic and diagnosed with bulimia nervosa. Which of the following psychotherapeutic interventions is the most eVective treatment in this age group?
questions.explanation:
Adolescents with bulimia nervosa may be treated with CBT adapted, as needed, to suit their age, circumstances, and level of development, and including the family as appropriate. NICE advises considering bulimia-nervosa-focused guided self-help (using cognitive behavioural materials) supplemented with brief supportive sessions. If this is unacceptable or ineVective after 4 weeks, consider individual CBT-ED for bulimia nervosa.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 693.
National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. NICE guideline Eating Disorders: recognition and treatment 2017.

questions.question_text: Which of the following sleep-wake disorders is associated with the use of stimulants?
questions.explanation:
Sleep-related bruxism is characterised by clenching and grinding of the teeth during sleep. It may result in temporomandibular joint pain, wearing down of the teeth, and/or injury to the tongue or mouth. It is most common at the transition to sleep, in stage 2 sleep, and during REM sleep. It may be related to stress and/or anxiety, dentition abnormalities, sleep-related breathing disorders, the use of stimulants, alcohol ingestion, and treatment with some SSRIs.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 476.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 501-502.

questions.question_text: Of those listed, the most common blood abnormality in adolescents with anorexia nervosa is
questions.explanation:
Anaemia, leukopenia, and although less frequently, thrombocytopaenia are possible haematological complications of anorexia nervosa (AN) considered strictly secondary to chronic malnutrition. Usually, anaemia in AN is normocytic and normochromic, and leukopenia is characterised by lymphocytopenia or neutropenia; thrombocytopaenia may also be present.
Ref: De Filippo E et al. Hematological complications in anorexia nervosa. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2016 Nov;70(11):1305-8.

questions.question_text: Report cards may be used as a tool in the treatment of which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation:
Research suggests that daily report cards are eVective in treating a range of ADHD symptoms and improving school outcomes, including academic achievement in some cases. This intervention typically involves teachers evaluating a student's behaviour at school against pre-determined targets, and parents subsequently providing reinforcement at home for positive reports.
Ref: Moore DA et al. Daily report cards as a school-based intervention for children with attention-de`cit/hyperactivity disorder. Support for Learning. 2016 Feb;31(1):71-83.

questions.question_text: Despite early behavioural interventions, the symptoms in autism spectrum disorder that tend not to improve over time are related to
questions.explanation:
Autism spectrum disorder is typically a lifelong, albeit heterogeneous disorder with highly variable severity and prognosis. Early intensive behavioural interventions can have a profoundly positive impact (in some cases, can lead to recovery and function in the average range). The symptoms that do not seem to improve substantively over time with early behavioural interventions are related to ritualistic and repetitive behaviours. Speci`cally, repetitive sensorimotor behaviours appear to be common, consistent, and potentially severe.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 127.
International Statistical Classi`cation of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is included in the ICD-11 description of autism spectrum disorder?

options.text: A particular interest in collecting things
Limitations in the sharing of interests with others

correct_answer.text: Limitations in the sharing of interests with others

correct_answers.text: Limitations in the sharing of interests with others

questions.explanation:
According to ICD-11, essential features of autism spectrum disorder include persistent de`cits in initiating and sustaining social communication and reciprocal social interactions that are outside the expected range of functioning given the individual's age and level of intellectual development. Manifestations may include limitations in the mutual sharing of interests with others.
Ref: International Statistical Classi`cation of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Which of the following symptoms is rare in early-onset schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Prodromal symptoms of early-onset schizophrenia can include odd ideas, eccentric interests, change in aVect, and unusual or bizarre perceptual experiences. Early-onset schizophrenia is characterised by a more insidious onset, negative symptoms, greater disorganisation (incoherence of thought and disordered sense of self), hallucinations in different modalities and, for relatively fewer patients, systematised or persecutory delusions. Catatonia is seldom seen.
Ref: Hollis C. Schizophrenia in children and adolescents. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Sep;21(5):333-41.
Harvey PD, Isner EC. Cognition, social cognition, and functional capacity in early-onset schizophrenia. Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Clinics. 2020 Jan 1;29(1):171-82.

questions.question_text: What is the medication of choice for an 8-year-old child with ADHD and tics?
questions.explanation:
Atomoxetine is a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor commonly prescribed for ADHD in children over 6 years of age. Unlike stimulants approved for ADHD, atomoxetine does not have abuse potential and may not exacerbate co-morbid tics. It can be given once a day in the morning.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber's Guide, 7 Edition. 2021. pp. 79-83.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best treatment option for a teenager with ADHD and ongoing substance use?
questions.explanation:
Atomoxetine is a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor commonly prescribed for ADHD. Unlike stimulants approved for ADHD, atomoxetine does not have abuse potential and may be useful where stimulant diversion is a problem.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber's Guide, 7 Edition. 2021. pp. 79-83.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 574.

questions.question_text: Asperger syndrome is characterised by all of the following except

options.text: Impaired awareness of the feeling of others
Impaired intellectual ability and syntactical speech

correct_answer.text: Impaired intellectual ability and syntactical speech

correct_answers.text: Impaired intellectual ability and syntactical speech

questions.explanation:
Asperger syndrome was `rst described by Hans Asperger in 1944, but only eponymously named in 1981 by Lorna Wing. It is characterised by severe persistent impairment in reciprocal social interactions, repetitive behaviour patterns, and restricted interests. There is impairment in social relatedness, as well as repetitive and stereotyped patterns of behaviour, without delay or marked aberrant language development and usage. Cognitive abilities and signi`cant adaptive skills are age-appropriate, although social communication is impaired. IQ and language are normal or, in some cases, superior.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 820.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 122.

questions.question_text: By the age of 18 years, what is the cumulative incidence of major depression?
questions.explanation:
Depressive disorders increase in frequency with increasing age in the general population. By age 18 years, the cumulative incidence of major depression is 20%. Among psychiatrically hospitalised children and adolescents, rates of major depressive disorder are close to 20% for children and 40% for adolescents.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 179.

questions.question_text: The most common adverse outcome of conduct disorder is the development of which of the following conditions in adulthood?
questions.explanation:
Around half of children with conduct disorder will receive a diagnosis of antisocial personality disorder as adults.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 665.

questions.question_text: The common presentations of anxiety disorders in preschool children include
questions.explanation:
Anxiety symptoms vary with age. Tearfulness and clinging in preschool children. Somatic complaints and hypochondriacal fretting are common in middle childhood (5-12) as are irritability and aggressive behaviour. Separation anxiety disorder and speci`c phobia usually have onset in early childhood.
Ref: Klein B, et al. Anxiety in children and youth: Part 1—Diagnosis. Paediatrics & Child Health. 2023 Feb;28(1):45-51.

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorders is among the most common psychiatric presentations seen in adolescents?
questions.explanation:
Anxiety disorders are among the most common psychiatric disorders in youth. Prevalence rates range from 5-15%, with 8% requiring clinical treatment.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 683.

questions.question_text: Which of the following adolescent-onset disorders was inaccurately portrayed as one of the "diseases of axuence" in the past?
questions.explanation:
Anorexia was considered to be more common among upper social class since its earliest description and social disadvantage was not seen as a strong determinant (Kendell 1973). It was grouped along with other "diseases of affluence" (Bruch, 1975), a term used to describe illnesses with elevated prevalence among populations with the highest incomes. This notion was first seen in seminal texts including that of Fenwick (1880) who observed that anorexia was "much more common in the wealthier class of society than amongst those who have to procure their bread by daily labor" with Bruch (1978) later describing it as a disease that "affects young and healthy girls who have been raised in privileged, even luxurious circumstances" . But it is increasingly recognised that this inference arose erroneously from sampling bias. A recent review of 62 articles published from 1973 to 2020 indicates that there is no pattern of evidence for a relationship between higher social status (of parents or adolescents) and eating disorders. Eating disorders present across a wide range of socioeconomic backgrounds (Huryk et al., 2021).
Ref: Huryk KM, Drury CR, Loeb KL. Diseases of axuence? A systematic review of the literature on socioeconomic diversity in eating disorders. Eating Behaviors. 2021 Dec 1;43:101548.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is least likely to be associated with PANDAS?
questions.explanation:
Paediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder associated with streptococcal infections (PANDAS) is characterised by the sudden and dramatic onset of obsessive-compulsive disorder, tic symptoms, or severely restricted food intake and neuropsychiatric comorbidity, also of sudden and severe onset, following group A streptococci (GAS) infection. Common comorbidities include anxiety (including separation anxiety); emotional lability and/or depression; irritability, aggression and/or severely oppositional behaviours; behavioural (developmental) regression; deterioration in school performance (ADHD-like symptoms, memory de`cits, cognitive changes); sensory or motor abnormalities; somatic signs and symptoms (including sleep disturbances, enuresis, or increased urinary frequency). Nearly ⅓ of children endorse concerns related to suicide. The term Pediatric Acute-onset Neuropsychiatric Syndrome (PANS) is used when the etiology or mechanism of the abrupt onset is unknown.
Ref: Warrilow A, Morton M. Autoimmune disorders in child psychiatry: keeping up with the `eld. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Nov;21(6):367-76.
Cabrera-Mendoza B et al. Diagnosis in PANDAS: An Update. Current Psychiatry Research and Reviews Formerly: Current Psychiatry Reviews. 2019 Dec 1;15(4):237-47.

questions.question_text: Seizures and irregular respiration are common features of
questions.explanation:
Rett Syndrome:
·       Believed to be caused by dominant X-linked gene
·       Degenerative disorder that almost exclusively affects females
·       Initially normal development
·       Ages 1-4 yrs: purposeful hand movements & spoken language lost; stereotypical hand movements (hand-wringing) & autism
·       Ataxia, facial grimacing, teeth-grinding, and loss of speech
·       Irregular respiration with episodes of hyperventilation, apnea, and breath-holding
·       Progressive gait disturbance, scoliosis, and seizures
·       Sleep disturbances are common; initial and/or intermediate insomnia, leading to excessive daytime sleep
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 103.
Persico AM et al. The psychopharmacology of autism spectrum disorder and Rett syndrome. In Handbook of clinical neurology 2019 Jan 1 (Vol. 165, pp. 391-414). Elsevier.

questions.question_text: In the UK, which of the following drugs should be prescribed `rst in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder in childhood?
questions.explanation:
Sertraline (from age 6 years) and buvoxamine (from age 8 years) are the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) licensed in the UK for the treatment of OCD in young people. Studies spanning 20 years have established the efficacy of SSRIs in the paediatric population in placebo-controlled trials. Sertraline and buoxetine are equally effective, but buvoxamine may be less so. Paroxetine is not recommended for use in children and young people. On occasion, medications other than sertraline and buvoxamine may be used as 'off-label' preparations with suitable caution. NICE guidance for the treatment of OCD recommends the use of SSRIs before the use of clomipramine, because of clomipramine's propensity for side effects and need for cardiac monitoring.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 561-562.
National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on core interventions in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder. Updated 2020.

questions.question_text: The onset of oppositional de`ant disorder is generally between the ages of
questions.explanation:
Although ODD can begin as early as 3 years of age, it typically is noted by 8 years of age and usually not later than early adolescence.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 189.

questions.question_text: The chief diVerential medical problem to be excluded in children with encopresis is
questions.explanation:
The chief differential medical problem to be excluded in children with encopresis is aganglionic megacolon or Hirschsprung disease, in which a patient may have an empty rectum and no desire to defecate but may still have an overbow of feces. The disorder occurs in 1 in 5000 children; signs appear shortly after birth. Faulty nutrition is rarely the cause of encopresis with constipation and overbow incontinence. Other conditions are rare as well, including structural disease of the anus, rectum, and colon, adverse drug eVects, or non-gastrointestinal medical (endocrine or neurologic) disorders.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 482.

questions.question_text: Known risk factors for child abuse include all except

options.text: A parent `gure who is biologically unrelated to the child
A parent who was abused as a child

questions.explanation:
Individual poverty is a well-known risk factor for child maltreatment. An association between socioeconomic status and the risk of child maltreatment has been demonstrated based on local, neighbourhood, and larger-scale studies.
Ref: Imran S et al. Association between socioeconomic status and risk of hospitalization due to child maltreatment in the USA. Journal of investigative medicine. 2019 Feb 1;67(2):346-9.

questions.question_text: Melatonin is considered an eVective treatment for children with insomnia and learning dimculties. Which of the following signi`cantly improves on treatment with this drug?
questions.explanation:
All forms of insomnia are more common in children with learning dimculties, autism, ADHD, and sensory impairments (particularly visual). Although behavioural interventions should be the primary intervention and have a robust evidence base, exogenous melatonin is now the '`rst-line' medication prescribed for childhood insomnia. Melatonin has been shown to decrease sleep onset latency, increase total sleep time, and improve overall sleep quality. The eVects of melatonin on sleep are modest but do not appear to dissipate with continued melatonin use.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 593-594.

questions.question_text: What is the UK prevalence for ADHD in children?
questions.explanation:
The UK prevalence for ADHD is just under 5%; 3-4% in boys and just under 1% in girls (four times more common in boys).
Ref: Hill P. Attention-de`cit hyperactivity disorder in children and adolescents: Assessment and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jan;21(1):23-30.

questions.question_text: A 9-year-old girl with ADHD and frequent aggressive outbursts has not responded to trials of methylphenidate or guanfacine. A trial of which of the following medications is now indicated?
questions.explanation:
The initial treatment of children and youth with ADHD with disruptive and aggressive behaviour includes the use of psychosocial interventions and psychostimulants to treat core ADHD symptoms. Psychostimulants have demonstrated efficacy for overt and covert aggression, as well as oppositional behaviour and conduct problems in children with ADHD. If these strategies are ineffective, there is evidence to support the use of atomoxetine, guanfacine and clonidine for oppositional behaviour and conduct problems associated with ADHD. As the side eVect burden of these medications is lower than with antipsychotics, their use is preferable over risperidone. If adequate symptom control is not achieved with the use of atomoxetine, guanfacine or clonidine, or they are contraindicated or intolerable, a trial of risperidone may be attempted. If risperidone is ineffective there is very little evidence to support the use of other antipsychotics. In general, the use of second-generation antipsychotics for the treatment of ADHD is not recommended.
Ref: Sha`q S, Pringsheim T. Using antipsychotics for behavioral problems in children. Expert Opinion on Pharmacotherapy. 2018 Sep 2;19(13):1475-88.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 571.

questions.question_text: What proportion of 15- to 16-year-old adolescents admit to incidents of deliberate self-harm in the UK?
questions.explanation:
In one of the most well known studies on this issue (Hawton et al., 2002), actual incidents of deliberate self-harm were admitted by 6.9% of adolescents aged 15 to16 (11.2% in females and 3.2% in males). The prevalence of ideation was estimated to be far higher. With wider age range, this number becomes larger. Nearly 15.5% between ages 13-18 (Morey et al., 2017) and 18.8% between ages 16-17 (Kidger et al., 2012 ALSPAC cohort) report ever having self-harmed with median age of onset of 13 years. 
Ref: Rahman F et al. Risk factors for self-harm repetition in adolescents: A systematic review. Clinical psychology review. 2021 Aug 1;88:102048.
Morey Y, Mellon D, Dailami N, Verne J, Tapp A. Adolescent self-harm in the community: an update on prevalence using a self-report survey of adolescents aged 13–18 in England. Journal of Public Health. 2017 Mar 1;39(1):58-64.
Hawton K, Rodham K, Evans E, Weatherall R. Deliberate self harm in adolescents: self report survey in schools in England. Bmj. 2002 Nov 23;325(7374):1207-11.
Kidger J, Heron J, Lewis G, Evans J, Gunnell D. Adolescent self-harm and suicidal thoughts in the ALSPAC cohort: a self-report survey in England. BMC psychiatry. 2012 Dec;12:1-2.

questions.question_text: A 3-year-old child is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) due to her delayed language development, lack of social interaction, resistance to physical affection, and sensitivity to sounds. According to ICD-11, what is the severity of her ASD?
questions.explanation:
ICD-11 does not designate severity of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Instead, qualifiers may be listed including a co-occurring disorder of intellectual development, degree of functional language impairment, and loss of previously acquired skills. If limitations in intellectual abilities are present, a separate diagnosis of disorder of intellectual development (ID) should also be assigned, using the appropriate category to designate severity of ID (i.e., mild, moderate, severe, profound, provisional).
Ref: International Statistical Classi`cation of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding enuresis is true?

options.text: Most children remit over time in childhood
Behavioural treatments have no evidence base
The diagnosis can be made only after age 3

correct_answer.text: Most children remit over time in childhood

correct_answers.text: Most children remit over time in childhood

questions.explanation:
Enuresis is the repeated voiding of urine into a child's clothes or bed; the voiding may be involuntary or intentional. For the diagnosis to be made, a child must exhibit a developmental or chronological age of at least 5 years. Genetic factors play a role in the expression of enuresis, given that the emergence of enuresis is significantly higher in `rst-degree relatives. A child's risk for enuresis is more than seven times higher if their father was enuretic. Enuresis is often self-limited, and a relatively high rate of spontaneous remission occurs over time in childhood. A classical conditioning behavioural intervention with the bell (or buzzer) and pad (alarm) apparatus is generally the most effective treatment for nocturnal enuresis. Desmopressin, an antidiuretic compound that is available as an intranasal spray, has shown success in reducing enuresis.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 483-485.
